query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained load, progressive plastic deformation is controlled by stress-driven dislocation nucleation and accumulation at the nanoscale layer interfaces, which in turn trigger localized FCC-to-HCP phase transformation. This process is mediated by the extent of short-range order (SRO) at the interfaces, which modulates the stacking fault energy (SFE) and thus the ease of dislocation motion and phase transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating comprising alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers, with inherent local short-range order at the interfaces.
generation.intervention: Subject the multilayer coating to a sustained mechanical load at a controlled temperature where both dislocation activity and limited diffusion are active.
generation.conditions: Loading conditions set to initiate plastic deformation (beyond the elastic regime but below delamination limits) at moderate temperatures, ensuring that the multilayer structure is retained.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface regions enriched in short-range order that influence local stacking fault energies and act as barriers to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load, dislocations nucleate preferentially at the FCC/BCC interfaces. Dislocation pile-up at these interfaces builds local stress until a critical threshold is reached, triggering partial slip and the formation of HCP lamellae via stacking fault processes. The local SRO increases the local SFE, thereby delaying the onset of the FCC-to-HCP transformation. This staged response modulates the progressive plastic deformation and helps balance strength with deformation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline multilayer with low SRO (lower SFE), the multilayer with enhanced interfacial SRO will exhibit delayed onset of dislocation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation, lower creep strain rates, and a more gradual transition from elastic to plastic deformation under sustained loading.
generation.baseline: Multilayer coatings with minimal interfacial SRO, expected to activate dislocation motion and FCC-to-HCP phase transformation at lower strains, leading to higher creep rates and more abrupt plastic deformation.
generation.boundary: Observations are valid under sustained loads before catastrophic coating failure or delamination and in temperature regimes where both dislocation slip and limited diffusion-driven processes are active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical stress or strain necessary to trigger the phase transformation and the quantitative effect of varying SRO on SFE and dislocation dynamics remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy multilayer coatings: one engineered to enhance interfacial short-range order (via controlled alloying and annealing) and one with reduced SRO (via rapid quenching). Under identical sustained loading and temperature conditions, monitor the progression of plastic deformation using in-situ techniques (e.g., transmission electron microscopy or synchrotron-based diffraction) to track dislocation activity and any localized FCC-to-HCP phase transformation at the interfaces.
measurements: Onset strain and stress for dislocation nucleation at interfaces
Dislocation density and pile-up magnitude near the interfaces
Spatial and temporal evolution of HCP phase formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the SRO-enhanced and SRO-reduced coatings exhibit similar onset of dislocation pile-up, FCC-to-HCP transformation, and creep strain rates, independent of expected differences in stacking fault energy, then the hypothesis that interfacial SRO modulates progressive plastic deformation via these mechanisms will be falsified.

In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

cited_evidence.text: Notably, quantitative analysis reveals that edge dislocations (26–30 counts) consistently outnumber screw dislocations (17–22 counts) across all testing temperatures. This behavior contrasts with the screw dislocation-dominated plasticity typically observed in conventional BCC metals and suggests a distortion-induced shift in the dominant deformation mechanism. The relatively high density of randomly distributed edge segments with multiple slip vectors promotes frequent dislocation interactions and entanglements. These entangled substructures serve as effective barriers that counteract the thermal softening typically observed during single-slip deformation at high temperatures, thereby suppressing strain localization and promoting more uniform deformation. Furthermore, pronounced dislocation interactions significantly restrict dislocation motion and enhance the likelihood of dislocation multiplication. cited_evidence.text: In this process, twin boundaries pose a barrier to dislocations shearing across the interface, while simultaneously redirecting the shear parallel to the interface, thereby forming hcp laths at the twin boundary. In addition, the hcp layers can form by glide of extended dislocations on adjacent planes, which is facilitated by the negative average stacking fault energy of the alloy. The coherent interface between hcp and fcc phases also stops and redirects the incoming dislocations, providing an additional strengthening source. Strong interface barriers such as large angle grain boundaries ordinarily would be expected to cause highly localized stress concentrations at the tips of dislocation pile-ups that could lead to premature crack initiation. Conversely, while the twin/hcp lath structures provides a strong barrier to slip transmission, the redirection of dislocations along the boundary smears out the damaging stress concentrations. With increasing strain, unusually large lattice rotations (greater than 30°) are created within individual grains, which further support the process described.
